ELIPPS: Exact Learning for Inverse Problems
from Partial Self-supervision

Benjamin Walder Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria    Markus Haltmeier Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria    Lukas Neumann Affiliation: Institute of Basic Sciences in Engineering Science, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria    Nadja Gruber Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Innsbruck, Innsbruck, Austria    Gyeongha Hwang ††thanks: Corresponding author: ghhwang@yu.ac.kr Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Yeungnam University, Gyeongsan, Republic of Korea
September 2026
Abstract

In undersampled inverse problems (such as sparse-view computed tomography), only a small number of measurements are collected, which reduces radiation exposure and acquisition time and cost, and can also address the inaccessibility of certain acquisition arrangements. Most learning-based methods for such problems require supervision in the form of fully sampled measurements and ground-truth images, which are costly or even infeasible to acquire. To overcome this issue, we propose Exact Learning for Inverse Problems from Partial Self-supervision (ELIPPS), an incomplete self-supervised training paradigm for undersampled inverse problems that requires neither ground-truth images nor fully sampled measurements. ELIPPS learns solely from incomplete forward measurements on a fixed incomplete supervision set. Our theory shows that when the data distribution is invariant under certain transformations, minimizing a masked empirical risk is equivalent to minimizing the full self-supervised risk, i.e. the risk against the complete, noise-free measurement. The equivalence is exact for arbitrary equivariant hypothesis classes and holds for signal-dependent noise such as the pre-log Poisson statistics of low-dose tomography, and for the log-transformed count model up to a quantifiable bias. When the underlying coverage condition is only approximately satisfied on a discrete grid, we give a stability estimate in terms of the associated frame constants and the irreducible error of the inverse problem. We realize ELIPPS for computed tomography by exploiting rotation and reflection invariance. In our experiments, ELIPPS substantially outperforms naive masked supervision and reaches the same order of accuracy as a reference model trained with full clean measurements.

Keywords: self-supervised learning, inverse problems, equivariance, computed tomography, sparse-view reconstruction, conditional expectation.

Mathematics Subject Classification: 65R32, 68T07, 94A08, 44A12.

1 Introduction

We study undersampled discrete inverse problems in which an unknown signal x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is observed through incomplete and noisy indirect measurements. Let A:ℝN→ℝMA:\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} denote the full forward operator. For I⊆{1,…,M}I\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\}, let PI:ℝM→ℝIP_{I}:\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{I} be the subsampling operator that selects the coordinates indexed by II, defined by PI​z=(zi)i∈IP_{I}z=(z_{i})_{i\in I}. Denote the subsampled forward operator by AI:=PI​AA_{I}:=P_{I}A. The undersampled inverse problem reads

yI=AI​x+ϵI,y_{I}=A_{I}x+\epsilon_{I}, (1.1)

where ϵI∈ℝI\epsilon_{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{I} is additive measurement noise. The objective is to recover the underlying image xx from the incompletely sampled measurements yI∈ℝIy_{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{I}. Problem (1.1) is challenging due to both the ill-posedness of inverting AA and the incompleteness of the sampling process.

A prominent example for (1.1) is sparse-view computed tomography (CT), where the full forward operator AA corresponds to the Radon transform mapping an image to its projection measurements (sinogram). In practical CT systems, measurements are often incomplete or limited due to sparse-view acquisition, detector subsampling, or low-dose scanning, which are commonly employed to reduce radiation exposure and acquisition time. These constraints make the reconstruction problem severely ill-posed and can introduce strong artifacts when classical reconstruction methods are applied directly.

Self-supervised reconstruction:

Learning-based reconstruction methods have achieved remarkable performance for inverse problems, including (1.1). Most approaches are supervised and assume access to paired training data (yI,x)(y_{I},x). In practice, collecting xx is challenging; typically even during training one only has access to additional measurements yS=AS​x+ϵSy_{S}=A_{S}x+\epsilon_{S}, where S⊆{1,…,M}S\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\} is the supervision set and AS=PS​AA_{S}=P_{S}A. Inspired by self-supervised learning for denoising [1, 2, 3], several self-supervised strategies have been proposed that use only measurements of ySy_{S}. Self-supervised reconstruction methods can be roughly classified into: (i) methods with full self-supervision (AS=AA_{S}=A; at least in expectation), e.g., [4, 5, 6]; and (ii) methods with sparse self-supervision (AS=AIA_{S}=A_{I}), e.g., [7, 8, 9, 10]. The setting studied in this paper is a third class, partial self-supervision, in which AS=PS​AA_{S}=P_{S}A for a supervision set SS that is fixed across acquisitions. Full self-supervision requires additional scans, higher radiation dose, or sensing configurations unavailable at deployment. Training with sparse self-supervision suffers from incomplete coverage of the data distribution, which can induce non-uniqueness and reliance on implicit priors. A recurring mechanism in this literature is measurement splitting: the acquired data are divided into an input part and a target part, and the network is trained to predict the latter from the former. This is the idea behind self-supervised reconstruction in MRI [11] and its analysis via variable-density resampling [6], and it is the measurement-domain counterpart of training against a second noisy realization as in Noise2Noise [12]. What distinguishes our setting from all of the above is that the split is neither random nor varying: the index sets II and SS are fixed once and for all by the acquisition.

A different line of research that leverages invariance is equivariant imaging (EI) [13, 14], which learns a reconstruction from the undersampled measurements yIy_{I} by enforcing equivariance of the measurement–reconstruction pipeline through an additional training penalty. Equivariant splitting [15] uses invariance of the signal distribution to reinterpret a single measurement as a measurement of a transformed signal through a transformed operator; see [16] for a comprehensive account of this field. Our setting differs from this line of work in two main respects. First, we assume partial self-supervision (1.2) on a fixed, deterministic supervision set SS, as opposed to unsupervised losses or random measurement splits, whose analysis requires sufficient diversity of the sampling patterns. Fixed SS reflects acquisition designs in which the retained measurement subset is determined by the hardware and identical across samples. Second, we do not promote equivariance through a penalty term but enforce it exactly by architectural symmetrization. Under a frame-type coverage condition we prove that the partially self-supervised risk and the full self-supervised risk are equivalent (Theorem 2.11), and we analyse when restricting the hypothesis class in this way costs nothing.

Partial self-supervision:

We propose an incomplete self-supervised setting for (1.1). For a fixed set S⊆{1,…,M}S\subseteq\left\{1,\dots,M\right\} we assume training data

(yI,yS)=(AI​x+ϵI,AS​x+ϵS),(y_{I},y_{S})=\bigl(A_{I}x+\epsilon_{I},\,A_{S}x+\epsilon_{S}\bigr), (1.2)

i.e., pairs of undersampled measurements yIy_{I} on the fixed set II as in (1.1) together with an incomplete measurement AS​x+ϵSA_{S}x+\epsilon_{S} on the fixed set SS. Such partial self-supervision arises when the retained subset of measurements is fixed by the acquisition design. In CT practice this is the case, for instance, when the set of projection angles is restricted by hardware, acquisition-time or dose constraints, or when a fixed, deliberately chosen part of the detector is read out at full resolution while the remainder is not. In all of these cases fully sampled reference measurements are unavailable even at training time, so that neither supervised learning nor full self-supervision is applicable.

As a concrete application, consider in-line industrial CT as illustrated in Figure 1.1. Here II and SS are separated by the acquisition itself rather than by a choice of dose. Source and detector are fixed and the part is carried past them on a conveyor, so that the belt position takes the role of the view direction and the position on the detector line that of the detector coordinate. Moving the detector away from the source leaves the number of detector elements unchanged but narrows the fan they cover, so that the same line samples a smaller part of the fan more finely. In production the detector sits close, giving a coarse measurement yIy_{I} over the whole fan; for calibration or first-article inspection it is moved back once, giving a fine measurement ySy_{S} over part of it. Both sets are fixed by the machine settings and neither contains the other. Parts that pass through both settings provide the training pairs (1.2); at deployment only yIy_{I} exists. Parts arrive in arbitrary in-plane orientation, so that the invariance of the signal distribution is a property of the application rather than one enforced by augmentation.

Learning under partial self-supervision is underdetermined: a regression loss that penalizes discrepancies only on the observed subset defined by PSP_{S} leaves the other coordinates unconstrained. As a result, models trained with naive self-supervision produce reconstructions that are locally consistent but globally inconsistent or artifact-prone. While [17] showed that noise-free inpainting (A=IdA=\operatorname{Id} and ϵI=0\epsilon_{I}=0) can be solved from incomplete supervision (1.2), by exploiting equivariance of the restoration map that fills in the missing data, the general case of incomplete, indirect observations with noise remains open. The step from that setting to the present one is not merely one of generality. With A=IdA=\operatorname{Id} the measurement and image domains coincide and the initial reconstruction is the identity, so that neither the interplay between transformations of the two domains nor the question of whether the admitted class of image-domain restoration maps is rich enough arises. Moreover, with AA ill-posed, noise is a major source of difficulty: the amplification of small perturbations makes the inverse problem challenging, and a noise-free model would miss this issue. The target of the masked regression is then no longer the clean signal: without noise the conditional expectation coincides with XX wherever the observation determines it, with noise it does not.

Main contributions:

We propose ELIPPS for (1.1) with incomplete self-supervised data (1.2). Our approach leverages invariance properties of the signal class together with intertwining relations of the forward map AA to enforce equivariance of the learned reconstruction with respect to known transformations. The key result shows that, over an equivariant function class, minimizing the partially self-supervised risk 𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}\,g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr] is equivalent to minimizing the full self-supervised risk 𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]. This enables globally consistent learning from partial self-supervision. We instantiate the approach for CT using detector upscaling (subsampling along the detector axis) and sparse-view reconstruction (subsampling along the angular axis).

Specific results: (i) A framework built on invariances of the signal class and intertwining relations of the forward operator, with a proof that masked regression over an equivariant class is equivalent to the full self-supervised risk (Theorem 2.11). ((ii) A characterization of the admissible supervision sets: a coverage condition on the transformed copies of SS is necessary as well as sufficient for the two risks to be proportional, and it bounds how small SS can be by the number of transformations and by the stabilizers of the action (Propositions 2.14 and 2.15). (iii) A network construction that enforces equivariance by design and applies to any modality whose forward operator intertwines with the transformations (Theorem 2.20), with a proof that this restriction does not change the minimizer (Theorem 2.23, Corollary 2.28), a counterexample showing which property of the initial reconstruction cannot be dropped (Remark 2.27), and an exact expression for what is lost when that property fails (Proposition 2.25). (iv) An exactness result for arbitrary equivariant hypothesis classes, which separates the correctness of the training criterion from the expressivity of the architecture (Corollary 2.13), and a stability estimate for an only approximately satisfied coverage condition (Theorem 2.17). (v) The combination of these results into the statement used in practice, namely that the minimizer over the trained architecture class is the conditional expectation (Corollary 2.29) and that the learned reconstruction agrees with the minimum mean squared error estimator up to ker⁡(A)\ker(A) (Corollary 2.30), together with a practical training objective and implementation (Section 2.5, equation (2.5)), realized for CT under low-dose Poisson noise and severe undersampling, reaching the accuracy of a reference model trained with full clean measurements (Section 3, Table 3.1). (vi) An ablation on the role of the symmetry of the training distribution (Section 3.7, Table 3.2).

Figure 1.2 summarizes the training setup and the reconstruction pipeline.

2 Incomplete Self-Supervised Learning

In this section we introduce and analyze Exact Learning for Inverse Problems from Partial Self-supervision (ELIPPS) for solving (1.1) using partial self-supervision (1.2). We adopt a probabilistic setting on a common probability space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}): the unknown image xx is the realization of a random vector (RV) XX with unknown distribution; the observed subsampled measurements are YI=AI​X+ϵIY_{I}=A_{I}X+\epsilon_{I} and the supervision measurement is YS=AS​X+ϵSY_{S}=A_{S}X+\epsilon_{S}. All expectations are taken with respect to the joint distribution induced by (1.1) and (1.2). For RVs Y,ZY,Z we write Y=dZY\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}Z for equality in distribution and Y=ZY=Z for almost sure equality (unless indicated otherwise, almost surely always refers to ℙ\mathbb{P}). Throughout, we write ℝI\mathbb{R}^{I} for the coordinate space indexed by II and identify ℝI≃ℝI×{0}⊆ℝM\mathbb{R}^{I}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{I}\times\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{M}, so that the orthogonal projector PIP_{I} acts as a binary masking operator on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}, zeroing out the coordinates outside II; analogously for SS.

2.1 Preliminaries

Let T:ℝM→ℝMT:\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} be an invertible linear map. The first key ingredient of ELIPPS is invariance of the underlying signal class.

Definition 2.1 (TT-invariant RV).

Let T:ℝM→ℝMT:\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} be an invertible linear map. A RV YY on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M} is said to be invariant with respect to TT (or TT-invariant, in distribution) if Y=dT⁡(Y)Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}T(Y).

Note that Y=dT⁡(Y)Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}T(Y) is much weaker than Y=T⁡(Y)Y=T(Y). Consider a distribution of images that is invariant under a rotation TT by 90∘90^{\circ}, for instance because every orientation of every image occurs with the same probability. Then Y=dT⁡(Y)Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}T(Y), whereas T⁡(Y)=YT(Y)=Y would require every single image to be unchanged by the rotation, which holds only for rotationally symmetric images. We write πY\pi_{Y} for the law of YY, i.e. πY​(E)=ℙ⁡(Y∈E)\pi_{Y}(E)=\mathbb{P}(Y\in E) for Borel sets E⊆ℝME\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{M}. In this notation the TT-invariance of YY reads πT⁡(Y)=πY\pi_{T(Y)}=\pi_{Y}, or equivalently ℙ⁡(Y∈E)=ℙ⁡(T⁡(Y)∈E)\mathbb{P}(Y\in E)=\mathbb{P}(T(Y)\in E) for all EE Borel.

Definition 2.2 (Joint TT-invariance).

Let Y,ZY,Z be RVs on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}. The pair (Z,Y)(Z,Y) is said to be jointly TT-invariant in distribution if (Z,Y)=d(T⁡(Z),T⁡(Y))(Z,Y)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(T(Z),T(Y)).

Besides invariance of the of RVs, we also use invariance of the sampling set II.

Definition 2.3 (TT-invariant subsampling).

We say that the sampling set I⊆{1,…,M}I\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\} is TT-invariant if PI​T=T​PIP_{I}T=TP_{I}.

Remark 2.4.

The commutation PI​T=T​PIP_{I}T=TP_{I} holds precisely when TT is block-diagonal with respect to ℝM=ℝI×ℝJ\mathbb{R}^{M}=\mathbb{R}^{I}\times\mathbb{R}^{J} with J={1,…,M}∖IJ=\{1,\dots,M\}\setminus I; that is, when TT maps the observed coordinates among themselves and likewise the unobserved ones. For a permutation TT this means that II is a union of cycles of TT, and then so is JJ automatically; this is how PI​T=T​PIP_{I}T=TP_{I} is verified in Section 3. For the main results it suffices to assume joint invariance directly, without the commutativity. We state the latter explicitly because it is what the sufficient condition of Lemma 2.5 and the sample-wise identity of Proposition 2.14 use.

Lemma 2.5 (Sufficient conditions for joint invariance).

Let YY be a RV on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}, let I⊆{1,…,M}I\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\}, and let YI=PI​Y+ϵIY_{I}=P_{I}Y+\epsilon_{I} with ϵI\epsilon_{I} independent of YY. Assume that YY and ϵI\epsilon_{I} are TT-invariant and that II is a TT-invariant sampling set. Then the pair (YI,Y)(Y_{I},Y) is jointly TT-invariant.

Proof.

Since ϵI\epsilon_{I} is independent of YY and TT is deterministic, T​ϵIT\epsilon_{I} is independent of T​YTY. Both pairs (Y,ϵI)(Y,\epsilon_{I}) and (T​Y,T​ϵI)(TY,T\epsilon_{I}) therefore have product laws, and their marginals agree because Y=dT​YY\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}TY and ϵI=dT​ϵI\epsilon_{I}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}T\epsilon_{I}; hence (Y,ϵI)=d(T​Y,T​ϵI)(Y,\epsilon_{I})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(TY,T\epsilon_{I}). Applying the measurable map (y,e)↦(PI​y+e,y)(y,e)\mapsto(P_{I}y+e,\,y) to both sides gives (YI,Y)=d(PI​(T​Y)+T​ϵI,T​Y)(Y_{I},Y)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\bigl(P_{I}(TY)+T\epsilon_{I},\,TY\bigr). Since II is TT-invariant and TT is linear, PI​(T​Y)+T​ϵI=T⁡(PI​Y+ϵI)=T​YIP_{I}(TY)+T\epsilon_{I}=T(P_{I}Y+\epsilon_{I})=TY_{I}, which is the claim. ∎

Definition 2.6 (Equivariance).

A function f:ℝM→ℝMf\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} is called TT-equivariant, for an invertible linear map TT, if f∘T=T∘ff\circ T=T\circ f. For a finite family 𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} of invertible linear maps, ff is called 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant if it is TℓT_{\ell}-equivariant for every ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\dots,L. The set of all measurable 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant functions f:ℝM→ℝMf\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} is denoted by Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}).

The conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[Y∣YI]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Y_{I}] depends on YIY_{I} only through the σ\sigma-algebra σ⁡(YI)=YI−1​(ℬ)\sigma(Y_{I})=Y_{I}^{-1}(\mathcal{B}) it generates. It is a random variable of the form h⁡(YI)h(Y_{I}) for a Borel function hh on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}, named Borel version of the regression function, written as h⁡(y)=𝔼⁡[Y∣YI=y]h(y)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Y_{I}=y], and determined only up to πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-null sets. Notice that the equivariance induced by joint invariance is a property of hh rather than of 𝔼⁡[Y∣YI]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Y_{I}]: since TT is invertible, σ⁡(T​YI)=σ⁡(YI)\sigma(TY_{I})=\sigma(Y_{I}), so nothing is gained at the level of the conditional expectation.

Lemma 2.7 (Joint invariance implies equivariance of the regression function).

Let (YI,Y)(Y_{I},Y) be jointly TT-invariant and square-integrable, and let h:ℝM→ℝMh\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} be a Borel version of the regression function h⁡(y)=𝔼⁡[Y∣YI=y]h(y)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Y_{I}=y]. Then h⁡(T​y)=T​h​(y)h(Ty)=T\,h(y) for πYI​-almost every ​y∈ℝM\pi_{Y_{I}}\text{-almost every }y\in\mathbb{R}^{M}.

Proof.

Since TT is deterministic and linear, a version of the regression function of T​YTY given T​YITY_{I} is y↦T​h​(T−1​y)y\mapsto T\,h(T^{-1}y); indeed, for every bounded Borel φ\varphi,

𝔼⁡[T​Y​φ​(T​YI)]=T​𝔼​[Y​φ​(T​YI)]=T​𝔼​[h⁡(YI)​φ​(T​YI)]=𝔼⁡[T​h​(T−1​(T​YI))​φ​(T​YI)].\mathbb{E}\bigl[TY\,\varphi(TY_{I})\bigr]=T\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y\,\varphi(TY_{I})\bigr]=T\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[h(Y_{I})\,\varphi(TY_{I})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[Th(T^{-1}(TY_{I}))\,\varphi(TY_{I})\bigr].

By joint TT-invariance, (T​YI,T​Y)=d(YI,Y)(TY_{I},TY)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(Y_{I},Y), so the two pairs have the same regression function up to a πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-null set; in particular πT​YI=πYI\pi_{TY_{I}}=\pi_{Y_{I}} and h⁡(y)=T​h​(T−1​y)h(y)=T\,h(T^{-1}y) for πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-almost every y∈ℝMy\in\mathbb{R}^{M} which is the assertion after replacing yy by T​yTy. ∎

Lemma 2.7 determines hh only up to a πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-null set, whereas Theorem 2.11 below minimizes over the class of everywhere defined equivariant maps. The gap is closed by symmetrization, which also explains why 𝒯\mathcal{T} is required to be a group (see Condition (A5) below).

Lemma 2.8 (Globally equivariant version).

Let 𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} be a finite group of invertible linear maps, let (YI,Y)(Y_{I},Y) be jointly TℓT_{\ell}-invariant for every ℓ\ell, and let hh be a Borel version of the regression function of YY given YIY_{I}. Then h~:=1L​∑ℓ=1LTℓ−1∘h∘Tℓ\tilde{h}:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}T_{\ell}^{-1}\circ h\circ T_{\ell} is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant and satisfies h~=h\tilde{h}=h πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-almost everywhere; in particular h~​(YI)=𝔼⁡[Y∣YI]\tilde{h}(Y_{I})=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Y_{I}] almost surely and h~∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\tilde{h}\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}).

Fix kk. Since 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a group, ℓ↦Tℓ​Tk\ell\mapsto T_{\ell}T_{k} permutes 𝒯\mathcal{T}, hence Tk−1∘h~∘Tk=1L​∑ℓ=1L(Tℓ​Tk)−1∘h∘(Tℓ​Tk)=h~T_{k}^{-1}\circ\tilde{h}\circ T_{k}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(T_{\ell}T_{k})^{-1}\circ h\circ(T_{\ell}T_{k})=\tilde{h}, so h~∘Tk=Tk∘h~\tilde{h}\circ T_{k}=T_{k}\circ\tilde{h} everywhere. 2.2 Measurement Self-supervision

We target the image restoration problem (1.1) of reconstructing a signal or image X∈ℝNX\in\mathbb{R}^{N} from incomplete, noisy, indirect observations. We consider a random setting with deterministic design and partial self-supervision (1.2). The method and main results are derived under the following assumptions.

Condition 2.9.

Assume the following hold:

  1. (A1)

    A:ℝN→ℝMA\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} is a fixed potentially nonlinear forward map.

  2. (A2)

    I,S⊆{1,…,M}I,S\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\} are fixed subsampling (input) and supervision index sets.

  3. (A3)

    The data are generated according to the partial self-supervision model (1.2).

  4. (A4)

    XX, ϵI\epsilon_{I} and ϵS\epsilon_{S} are square-integrable, and 𝔼[ϵS∣X,ϵI]=0\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{S}\mid X,\epsilon_{I}]=0.

  5. (A5)

    𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} is a finite group of invertible linear operators on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}, of order LL.

  6. (A6)

    For every ℓ\ell, the pair (YI,A​X)(Y_{I},AX) is jointly TℓT_{\ell}-invariant.

  7. (A7)

    There exists c>0c>0 such that for all v∈ℝM:∑ℓ=1L‖PS​Tℓ​v‖22=c​‖v‖22v\in\mathbb{R}^{M}\colon\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|P_{S}\,T_{\ell}v\|_{2}^{2}=c\,\|v\|_{2}^{2}.

Remark 2.10 (On the noise assumption (A4)).

The usual assumption in this context, that ϵS\epsilon_{S} be zero-mean and independent of (X,ϵI)(X,\epsilon_{I}), implies (A4), but not conversely. In particular, (A4) requires the noise neither to be additive nor signal-independent nor identically distributed across coordinates, and it imposes no assumption whatsoever on the joint law of XX and ϵI\epsilon_{I}. It is satisfied whenever the supervision measurement is an unbiased acquisition that is conditionally independent of the input acquisition given the signal: if 𝔼⁡[YS∣X]=AS​X\mathbb{E}[Y_{S}\mid X]=A_{S}X and YSY_{S} is conditionally independent of ϵI\epsilon_{I} given XX, then the latter gives 𝔼[YS∣X,ϵI]=𝔼[YS∣X]\mathbb{E}[Y_{S}\mid X,\epsilon_{I}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{S}\mid X], whence 𝔼[ϵS∣X,ϵI]=𝔼[YS−ASX∣X,ϵI]=𝔼[YS∣X]−ASX=0\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{S}\mid X,\epsilon_{I}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{S}-A_{S}X\mid X,\epsilon_{I}]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{S}\mid X]-A_{S}X=0. This covers signal-dependent noise, in particular Poisson statistics, and requires no Gaussian approximation. It does require the supervision measurement to be unbiased, which is not automatic: if the sinogram is formed from photon counts by a log transform, a systematic bias enters. Remark 2.12 below shows that such a bias propagates in a controlled way.

Note that Condition (A4) implies that the supervision measurement must not reuse the noise of the input measurement. Physically this leaves two options: either two conditionally independent acquisitions of the same object, in the spirit of Noise2Noise [12], or a single acquisition split into two independent parts, achieved for photon counts by Poisson thinning at unchanged total dose. A disjoint design I∩S=∅I\cap S=\emptyset would also suffice, but (A7) forces SS to meet every orbit while PI​Tℓ=Tℓ​PIP_{I}T_{\ell}=T_{\ell}P_{I} forces II to be a union of orbits, so the two sets must overlap; see Section 3.

Throughout, every minimization over a class of maps is understood to range over those gg in the class for which g⁡(YI)g(Y_{I}) is square-integrable. Identities between minimizers are understood in the usual L2L^{2} sense: the arg​min\argmin is the set of minimizers of the stated risk, all of whose elements agree πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-almost everywhere, and an equation of the form 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]=arg​min⁡(⋅)\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=\argmin(\cdot) asserts that every minimizer gg satisfies g⁡(YI)=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]g(Y_{I})=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] almost surely. Whether the minimum is attained is addressed by Lemma 2.8 and, for the constrained classes of Sections 2.3 and 2.4, by Corollary 2.28.

Theorem 2.11 (Exact learning from partial self-supervision).

Suppose Condition 2.9 holds. Then, over the equivariant function class Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}), minimizing the partially self-supervised noisy-target risk recovers the clean conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]=arg​ming∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)⁡𝔼​[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22].\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=\argmin_{g\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T})}\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}\,g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].
Proof.

Let Z=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]Z=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]; by Lemmas 2.7 and 2.8 (applied with Y=A​XY=AX) it is attained by a map in Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}). For any square-integrable g:ℝM→ℝMg:\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M}, expand the noisy-target risk:

𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−PS​A​X∥22]+𝔼⁡[∥ϵS∥22]−2​𝔼​[⟨PS​(g⁡(YI)−A​X),ϵS⟩].\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-P_{S}AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert\epsilon_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]-2\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\langle P_{S}(g(Y_{I})-AX),\epsilon_{S}\rangle\right].

Since g⁡(YI)−A​Xg(Y_{I})-AX is σ⁡(X,ϵI)\sigma(X,\epsilon_{I})-measurable, conditioning on (X,ϵI)(X,\epsilon_{I}) and using (A4) shows that the cross term vanishes. Since 𝔼⁡[∥ϵS∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert\epsilon_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr] does not depend on gg, minimizing the masked noisy risk is equivalent to minimizing the masked clean risk 𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−PS​A​X∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-P_{S}AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].

Let gg be 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant and define R=g⁡(YI)−A​XR=g(Y_{I})-AX. By equivariance, g⁡(Tℓ​YI)−Tℓ​A​X=Tℓ​Rg(T_{\ell}Y_{I})-T_{\ell}AX=T_{\ell}R; by joint invariance (Condition (A6)), 𝔼⁡[∥PS​R∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥PS​Tℓ​R∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}R\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}T_{\ell}R\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr] for all ℓ\ell. Averaging over ℓ\ell and using Condition (A7) yields

𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−PS​A​X∥22]=1L​𝔼​[∑ℓ=1L‖PS​Tℓ​R‖22]=cL​𝔼​[∥R∥22]=cL​𝔼​[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22].\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-P_{S}AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\frac{1}{L}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|P_{S}T_{\ell}R\|_{2}^{2}\right]=\frac{c}{L}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert R\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\frac{c}{L}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].

Therefore, within Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}), the masked clean risk is strictly proportional to the full clean risk, and both are minimized by Z=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]Z=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]. ∎

Remark 2.12 (Biased supervision).

Suppose that instead of (A4) the supervision noise satisfies 𝔼[ϵS∣X,ϵI]=PSβ(X)\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{S}\mid X,\epsilon_{I}]=P_{S}\,\beta(X) for a measurable bias map β:ℝN→ℝM\beta\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{M}, and that the pair (YI,A​X+β⁡(X))(Y_{I},AX+\beta(X)) is jointly TℓT_{\ell}-invariant for every ℓ\ell (which holds, for instance, when β\beta acts coordinatewise on A​xAx and the TℓT_{\ell} are coordinate permutations). Writing ϵS=PS​β​(X)+η\epsilon_{S}=P_{S}\beta(X)+\eta with 𝔼[η∣X,ϵI]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta\mid X,\epsilon_{I}]=0 and repeating the proof of Theorem 2.11 with A​XAX replaced by A​X+β⁡(X)AX+\beta(X) gives

arg​ming∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)⁡𝔼​[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22]=𝔼⁡[AX+β⁡(X)|YI].\argmin_{g\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T})}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[AX+\beta(X)\,\big|\,Y_{I}\bigr].

The minimizer of the partially self-supervised risk is therefore again a conditional expectation, now of the biased quantity A​X+β⁡(X)AX+\beta(X) instead of A​XAX: the learned predictor inherits the bias of the supervision measurement and nothing else. Its deviation from 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] is 𝔼⁡[β⁡(X)∣YI]\mathbb{E}[\beta(X)\mid Y_{I}], whose L2L^{2} norm is at most ‖β⁡(X)‖L2\|\beta(X)\|_{L^{2}} because conditional expectation is an L2L^{2} contraction. The latter can be estimated from a concrete acquisition model; see Section 3.

The proof gives more than the statement of Theorem 2.11: on the whole equivariant class the two risks differ only by a positive factor and an additive constant, which yields an exactness statement independent of any modelling assumption.

Corollary 2.13 (Exactness within arbitrary equivariant subclasses).

Suppose Condition 2.9 holds and let 𝒞⊆Equi⁡(ℝM;𝒯)\mathcal{C}\subseteq\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}) be an arbitrary nonempty class of square-integrable equivariant maps. Then

arg​ming∈𝒞⁡𝔼​[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22]=arg​ming∈𝒞⁡𝔼​[∥g⁡(YI)−𝔼⁡[AX∣YI]∥22],\argmin_{g\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}\,g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\argmin_{g\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr],

i.e. training on partially self-supervised, noisy data over 𝒞\mathcal{C} returns the best L2L^{2}-approximation of 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] available in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Proof.

Write Z=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]Z=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]. By the two displays in the proof of Theorem 2.11, every g∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)g\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}) satisfies 𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22]=cL​𝔼​[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22]+𝔼⁡[∥ϵS∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\frac{c}{L}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert\epsilon_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]. Since g⁡(YI)g(Y_{I}) is σ⁡(YI)\sigma(Y_{I})-measurable and 𝔼⁡[A​X−Z∣YI]=0\mathbb{E}[AX-Z\mid Y_{I}]=0, the Pythagoras identity for conditional expectations gives 𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−Z∥22]+𝔼⁡[∥A​X−Z∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-Z\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert AX-Z\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr], and the last term does not depend on gg. The two objectives therefore differ by the positive factor c/Lc/L and an additive constant, which do not change the set of minimizers. ∎

Corollary 2.13 makes ELIPPS robust with respect to modelling choices. Whatever the hypothesis class, minimizing the partially self-supervised risk over an equivariant class is therefore always equivalent to minimizing the full self-supervised risk over the same class. Assumptions beyond Condition 2.9, in particular those of Section 2.4, are never needed for the correctness of the training objective; they only decide whether 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] lies in the class.

Theorem 2.11 is a statement about expectations. When the training set is closed under the group action, a purely deterministic statement is available as well: on the orbit of a single sample, the masked loss and the full unmasked loss coincide.

Proposition 2.14 (Orbit identity).

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} satisfy (A7), let PI​Tℓ=Tℓ​PIP_{I}T_{\ell}=T_{\ell}P_{I} for every ℓ\ell, and let g∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)g\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}). For a measurement vector y∈ℝMy\in\mathbb{R}^{M} put yI=PI​yy_{I}=P_{I}y, and consider the orbit of yy under 𝒯\mathcal{T} with the associated input and supervision data yI(ℓ)=PI​Tℓ​yy_{I}^{(\ell)}=P_{I}T_{\ell}y and yS(ℓ)=PS​Tℓ​yy_{S}^{(\ell)}=P_{S}T_{\ell}y. Then

∑ℓ=1L‖PS​g​(yI(ℓ))−yS(ℓ)‖22=c​‖g⁡(yI)−y‖22.\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigl\|P_{S}\,g\bigl(y_{I}^{(\ell)}\bigr)-y_{S}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\;=\;c\,\bigl\|g(y_{I})-y\bigr\|_{2}^{2}.
Proof.

Since PIP_{I} commutes with TℓT_{\ell} we have yI(ℓ)=Tℓ​PI​y=Tℓ​yIy_{I}^{(\ell)}=T_{\ell}P_{I}y=T_{\ell}y_{I}, and equivariance of gg gives g⁡(yI(ℓ))=Tℓ​g​(yI)g(y_{I}^{(\ell)})=T_{\ell}\,g(y_{I}). Hence PS​g​(yI(ℓ))−yS(ℓ)=PS​Tℓ​vP_{S}g(y_{I}^{(\ell)})-y_{S}^{(\ell)}=P_{S}T_{\ell}v with v=g⁡(yI)−yv=g(y_{I})-y, and summing over ℓ\ell and using (A7) yields ∑ℓ‖PS​Tℓ​v‖22=c​‖v‖22\sum_{\ell}\|P_{S}T_{\ell}v\|_{2}^{2}=c\|v\|_{2}^{2}. ∎

The identity in Proposition 2.14 is exact and finite: it involves no probability distribution, no invariance assumption on the data and no expectation. If the training set is closed under the group action, the empirical masked risk over the orbit-closed set therefore equals cc times the empirical full risk over the original samples, for every equivariant candidate. Enlarging the training set by the group is thus not a way of obtaining more data but the finite realization of the coverage condition (A7), which the next proposition turns into a characterization. Theorem 2.11 is the expectation version of the same mechanism. There the noise contributes a cross term that vanishes only in the mean, which is precisely where (A4) and the joint invariance (A6) enter.

Proposition 2.15 (Characterization of the coverage condition).

Let 𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} be a finite set of invertible linear maps, not necessarily a group, and let S⊆{1,…,M}S\subseteq\{1,\dots,M\}. Then (A7) holds, that is ∑ℓ∥PS​Tℓ​v∥22=c​∥v∥22\sum_{\ell}\lVert P_{S}T_{\ell}v\rVert_{2}^{2}=c\,\lVert v\rVert_{2}^{2} for every v∈ℝMv\in\mathbb{R}^{M}, if and only if

∑ℓ=1LTℓ⊤​PS​Tℓ=c​Id.\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}T_{\ell}^{\!\top}P_{S}\,T_{\ell}=c\,\operatorname{Id}. (2.1)
Proof.

For every vv we have ∑ℓ∥PS​Tℓ​v∥22=∑ℓ⟨Tℓ⊤​PS⊤​PS​Tℓ​v,v⟩=⟨∑ℓTℓ⊤​PS​Tℓ​v,v⟩\sum_{\ell}\lVert P_{S}T_{\ell}v\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{\ell}\langle T_{\ell}^{\!\top}P_{S}^{\!\top}P_{S}T_{\ell}\,v,v\rangle=\langle\sum_{\ell}T_{\ell}^{\!\top}P_{S}T_{\ell}\,v,v\rangle, because PS⊤​PS=PSP_{S}^{\!\top}P_{S}=P_{S} for an orthogonal projection. A symmetric matrix is determined by its quadratic form, so this equals c​∥v∥22c\lVert v\rVert_{2}^{2} for all vv if and only if (2.1) holds. ∎

In the language of frame theory, (2.1) states that the rows of the maps (PS​Tℓ)ℓ=1L(P_{S}T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} form a tight frame of ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M} with frame constant cc. For orthogonal TℓT_{\ell}, taking traces gives |S|=c​M/L\lvert S\rvert=c\,M/L, which is the quantitative content of the condition: the supervision set must contain a fraction c/Lc/L of all measurements, so the achievable compression is bounded by LL. Under Condition 2.9, where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a group, LL is its order; for the dihedral group D4D_{4} used in Section 3 this is a factor of eight. Whether c=1c=1 is attainable depends on the action. If the TℓT_{\ell} are permutations and a coordinate ii is fixed by kk of them, then every coordinate that SS reaches in the same orbit contributes kk to the multiplicity of ii, so tightness forces c≥kc\geq k and hence |S|≥k​M/L\lvert S\rvert\geq k\,M/L. Only a free action, in which no coordinate is fixed by a nontrivial group element, admits c=1c=1 and |S|=M/L\lvert S\rvert=M/L. On a discrete grid the reflection axes of D4D_{4} produce fixed coordinates; the weighted formulation of Remark 2.16 removes the obstruction by counting them with the reciprocal of their multiplicity. Conversely, the condition tells us how to choose SS: as a fundamental domain of the group action, which is a design decision rather than something found in the data.

Remark 2.16 (Weighted supervision masks).

Let W∈ℝM×MW\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M} be a diagonal matrix with nonnegative entries supported in SS, and replace (A7) by the weighted coverage condition

∑ℓ=1L‖W1/2​PS​Tℓ​v‖22=c​‖v‖22for all ​v∈ℝM.\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigl\|W^{1/2}P_{S}\,T_{\ell}v\bigr\|_{2}^{2}=c\,\|v\|_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{for all }v\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. (A7W)

Then Theorem 2.11 and Corollary 2.13 remain valid verbatim for the weighted risk 𝔼⁡[∥W1/2​(PS​g​(YI)−YS)∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert W^{1/2}(P_{S}g(Y_{I})-Y_{S})\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]. Indeed, the only property of PSP_{S} used in the proofs is that it is a fixed deterministic linear map, so that R=dTℓ​RR\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}T_{\ell}R implies 𝔼⁡[∥W1/2​PS​R∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥W1/2​PS​Tℓ​R∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert W^{1/2}P_{S}R\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert W^{1/2}P_{S}T_{\ell}R\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]. The additional freedom is useful on discrete grids, where the group action typically has fixed points and an unweighted mask can be a fundamental domain only up to those fixed points; see Section 3.

Condition (A7) requires the transformed supervision sets to cover the measurement domain exactly. On a discrete grid this can fail by a small amount. The following stability estimate shows that the conclusion of Theorem 2.11 survives on the part of the measurement domain that is covered at all, no matter how unevenly.

Theorem 2.17 (Stability under approximate coverage).

Suppose Condition 2.9 holds with (A7) replaced by the following one-sided condition: there exist a constant c1>0c_{1}>0 and an orthogonal coordinate projection QQ on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M} such that

c1​‖Q​v‖22≤∑ℓ=1L‖PS​Tℓ​v‖22for all ​v∈ℝM.c_{1}\|Qv\|_{2}^{2}\;\leq\;\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\|P_{S}\,T_{\ell}v\|_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{for all }v\in\mathbb{R}^{M}. (2.2)

Let Z=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]Z=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] and let g^∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\hat{g}\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}) be a δ\delta-minimizer of the partially self-supervised risk, i.e. 𝔼⁡[∥PS​g^​(YI)−YS∥22]≤infg𝔼⁡[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22]+δ\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}\hat{g}(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]\leq\inf_{g}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]+\delta for some δ≥0\delta\geq 0. Then

𝔼⁡[∥Q⁡(g^​(YI)−Z)∥22]≤Lc1​δ.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert Q\bigl(\hat{g}(Y_{I})-Z\bigr)\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]\;\leq\;\frac{L}{c_{1}}\,\delta.

In particular, for δ=0\delta=0 the conditional expectation ZZ is identified exactly on the range of QQ.

Proof.

Write MS:=∑ℓ=1LTℓ⊤​PS​TℓM_{S}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}T_{\ell}^{\!\top}P_{S}\,T_{\ell}, so that ∑ℓ‖PS​Tℓ​v‖22=⟨MS​v,v⟩\sum_{\ell}\|P_{S}T_{\ell}v\|_{2}^{2}=\langle M_{S}v,v\rangle and (2.2) reads c1​‖Q​v‖22≤⟨MS​v,v⟩c_{1}\|Qv\|_{2}^{2}\leq\langle M_{S}v,v\rangle. For g∈Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)g\in\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}) put Rg=g⁡(YI)−A​XR_{g}=g(Y_{I})-AX and Dg=g⁡(YI)−ZD_{g}=g(Y_{I})-Z. As in the proof of Theorem 2.11 the noisy-target risk equals 𝔼⁡[∥PS​Rg∥22]+𝔼⁡[∥ϵS∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}R_{g}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert\epsilon_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr] and Rg=dTℓ​RgR_{g}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}T_{\ell}R_{g} for every ℓ\ell, so

L​𝔼​[∥PS​Rg∥22]=𝔼⁡[∑ℓ‖PS​Tℓ​Rg‖22]=𝔼⁡[⟨MS​Rg,Rg⟩].L\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}R_{g}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{\ell}\|P_{S}T_{\ell}R_{g}\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle M_{S}R_{g},R_{g}\rangle\bigr].

Decompose Rg=Dg+(Z−A​X)R_{g}=D_{g}+(Z-AX). Since DgD_{g} is σ⁡(YI)\sigma(Y_{I})-measurable, so is MS​DgM_{S}D_{g}, and 𝔼⁡[Z−A​X∣YI]=0\mathbb{E}[Z-AX\mid Y_{I}]=0, so the cross term vanishes and 𝔼⁡[⟨MS​Rg,Rg⟩]=𝔼⁡[⟨MS​Dg,Dg⟩]+𝔼⁡[⟨MS​(Z−A​X),Z−A​X⟩]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle M_{S}R_{g},R_{g}\rangle\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle M_{S}D_{g},D_{g}\rangle\bigr]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[\langle M_{S}(Z-AX),Z-AX\rangle\bigr], where the second term does not depend on gg. The risk is therefore, up to an additive constant, a quadratic form in DgD_{g} alone. By Lemma 2.8, applied with Y=A​XY=AX, the value ZZ is attained within Equi⁡(ℝM,𝒯)\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}), and there Dg=0D_{g}=0, so δ\delta-minimality of g^\hat{g} gives 𝔼⁡[⟨MS​Dg^,Dg^⟩]≤L​δ\mathbb{E}[\langle M_{S}D_{\hat{g}},D_{\hat{g}}\rangle]\leq L\delta. The lower bound in (2.2) now yields c1​𝔼​[∥Q​Dg^∥22]≤𝔼⁡[⟨MS​Dg^,Dg^⟩]≤L​δc_{1}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert QD_{\hat{g}}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]\leq\mathbb{E}[\langle M_{S}D_{\hat{g}},D_{\hat{g}}\rangle]\leq L\delta, which is the assertion. ∎

The proof applies (A7) only to the residual R=g⁡(YI)−A​XR=g(Y_{I})-AX, so requiring it on ran(A)\range(A) suffices for the factorized class of Section 2.3. This is a genuine weakening whenever AA has a nontrivial cokernel, but not for the discretization of Section 3, where ran(A)=ℝM\range(A)=\mathbb{R}^{M} is expected. The estimate depends on the multiplicities only through the lower bound c1c_{1}: uneven overlap of the images Tℓ​(S)T_{\ell}(S) reweights the risk but does not move its minimizer, and the conditional expectation is still identified exactly wherever (A7) fails only in this way. What cannot be repaired is a coordinate reached by no image at all, which is why QQ appears in the statement.

2.3 Self-supervised image reconstruction

We realize the optimal predictor of Theorem 2.11 as gθ=A∘fθ∘Bg_{\theta}=A\circ f_{\theta}\circ B with an image-space network fθ:ℝN→ℝNf_{\theta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}, a fixed initial reconstruction B:ℝM→ℝNB\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N} such as filtered backprojection, and the forward operator. 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariance of gθg_{\theta} is enforced through intertwining relations between the measurement-space transforms 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the image-space transforms 𝒮\mathcal{S}, together with symmetric averaging of fθf_{\theta} in image space.

Condition 2.18.

Let 𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=1L∈GL​(ℝM)L\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L}\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{R}^{M})^{L} and 𝒮=(Sℓ)ℓ=1L∈GL​(ℝN)L\mathcal{S}=(S_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L}\in\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{R}^{N})^{L} be finite families of invertible linear operators satisfying:

  1. 1.

    (Intertwining with AA) For all ℓ∈{1,…​L}\ell\in\{1,\dots L\}: Tℓ∘A=A∘SℓT_{\ell}\circ A\;=\;A\circ S_{\ell}

  2. 2.

    (Intertwining of BB) For all ℓ∈{1,…​L}\ell\in\{1,\dots L\}: B∘Tℓ=Sℓ∘BB\circ T_{\ell}\;=\;S_{\ell}\circ B

  3. 3.

    (Group structure) 𝒮=(Sℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{S}=(S_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} is a finite group of order LL.

Condition 2.18 is naturally satisfied in tomographic problems with known symmetries such as the Radon transform, where rotations in image space correspond to translations of the sinogram.

Remark 2.19 (Two opposite uses of a symmetry group).

Methods that learn from yIy_{I} alone use the invariance of the signal distribution to read the same data as a measurement of a transformed signal through a transformed operator. For that mechanism to supply information, the forward operator must not commute with the group, since otherwise all virtual operators share the null space of AA [18, 16]. Condition 2.18 asks for the intertwining Tℓ​A=A​SℓT_{\ell}A=AS_{\ell} to hold exactly, so we are in the regime that excludes it. There is no contradiction: here the supervision comes from ySy_{S}, and the group is not asked to produce new information but to transport the supervision that exists on SS across the measurement domain, which is what (A7) formalizes. Consistently, we make no claim about the null space; Corollary 2.30 identifies the reconstruction only modulo ker⁡(A)\ker(A).

Theorem 2.20.

For given linear B:ℝM→ℝNB\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}, let 𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} and 𝒮=(Sℓ)ℓ=1L\mathcal{S}=(S_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L} satisfy Condition 2.18. For any measurable Φ:ℝN→ℝN\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}, define

f\displaystyle f :ℝN→ℝN,f≔1L​∑ℓ=1LSℓ−1∘Φ∘Sℓ,\displaystyle\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N},\qquad f\coloneqq\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}S_{\ell}^{-1}\circ\Phi\circ S_{\ell}, (2.3)
g\displaystyle g :ℝM→ℝM,g≔A∘f∘B.\displaystyle\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M},\qquad g\coloneqq A\circ f\circ B\,. (2.4)

Then ff, and gg are 𝒮\mathcal{S}-equivariant and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant, respectively.

Proof.

Fix k∈{1,…,L}k\in\{1,\dots,L\}. Using the intertwining relations Tk​A=A​SkT_{k}A=AS_{k} and B​Tk=Sk​BBT_{k}=S_{k}B (Condition 2.18), we have

Tk∘g\displaystyle T_{k}\circ g =Tk∘(A∘f∘B)=A∘(Sk∘f)∘B,\displaystyle=T_{k}\circ(A\circ f\circ B)=A\circ(S_{k}\circ f)\circ B,
g∘Tk\displaystyle g\circ T_{k} =(A∘f∘B)∘Tk=A∘(f∘Sk)∘B.\displaystyle=(A\circ f\circ B)\circ T_{k}=A\circ(f\circ S_{k})\circ B.

Hence, it suffices to show that ff commutes with every SkS_{k}. Since 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a group, Sk−1∈𝒮S_{k}^{-1}\in\mathcal{S} and the assignment ℓ↦m⁡(ℓ)\ell\mapsto m(\ell) defined by Sm⁡(ℓ)=Sℓ∘Sk−1S_{m(\ell)}=S_{\ell}\circ S_{k}^{-1} is a bijection of {1,…,L}\{1,\dots,L\}. Using first the identity Sk∘Sℓ−1∘Φ∘Sℓ=((Sℓ∘Sk−1)−1∘Φ∘(Sℓ∘Sk−1))∘SkS_{k}\circ S_{\ell}^{-1}\circ\Phi\circ S_{\ell}=\bigl((S_{\ell}\circ S_{k}^{-1})^{-1}\circ\Phi\circ(S_{\ell}\circ S_{k}^{-1})\bigr)\circ S_{k}, which holds term by term, and then this reindexing, we obtain

Sk∘f=1L​∑ℓ=1LSk∘(Sℓ−1∘Φ∘Sℓ)=1L​∑ℓ=1L((Sℓ∘Sk−1)−1∘Φ∘(Sℓ∘Sk−1))∘Sk=1L​∑m=1L(Sm−1∘Φ∘Sm)∘Sk=f∘Sk,S_{k}\circ f=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}S_{k}\circ(S_{\ell}^{-1}\circ\Phi\circ S_{\ell})\\ =\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigl((S_{\ell}\circ S_{k}^{-1})^{-1}\circ\Phi\circ(S_{\ell}\circ S_{k}^{-1})\bigr)\circ S_{k}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{m=1}^{L}(S_{m}^{-1}\circ\Phi\circ S_{m})\circ S_{k}=f\circ S_{k}\,,

which concludes the proof. ∎

The averaging in (2.3) is the classical Reynolds operator, and its use to render a network equivariant is standard; it appears in the learning literature as group or frame averaging [19, 20, 21] and, for imaging, in test-time symmetrization of plug-and-play denoisers [22]. What is specific here is not the averaging itself but its combination with the forward operator and the initial reconstruction, together with the statement that the resulting restriction of the hypothesis class costs nothing (Theorem 2.23 and Corollary 2.28). No architectural constraints on Φ\Phi are required; equivariance is enforced purely by the symmetrization. Thus, Φ\Phi can be any CNN operating in image space. In practice, BB can be chosen as a standard analytic or approximate inverse (for example FBP for the Radon transform), which typically intertwines with rotations and reflections.

2.4 Architectural freedom

Realizing gθ=A∘fθ∘Bg_{\theta}=A\circ f_{\theta}\circ B guarantees the equivariance of the network by construction. In this subsection we show that this comes at no cost: the restriction to the factorized class leaves the solution of the minimization problem unchanged.

Definition 2.21 (Right-inverse and least-squares right-inverse).

Let A:ℝN→ℝMA\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} be a linear operator and Pran(A):ℝM→ℝMP_{\range(A)}\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} the orthogonal projection onto the range of AA. An operator B:ℝM→ℝNB\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N} is called a right-inverse of AA if A​B​y=yABy=y for all y∈ran(A)y\in\range(A) and a least-squares right-inverse of AA if, in addition, A​B​y=Pran(A)​(y)ABy=P_{\range(A)}(y) for all y∈ℝMy\in\mathbb{R}^{M}.

For a least-squares right-inverse, B​yBy is a least-squares solution of the equation A​x=yAx=y for every y∈ℝMy\in\mathbb{R}^{M}, since ‖A⁡(B​y)−y‖2=‖Pran(A)​(y)−y‖2=minx⁡‖A​x−y‖2\|A(By)-y\|_{2}=\|P_{\range(A)}(y)-y\|_{2}=\min_{x}\|Ax-y\|_{2}. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse A†A^{\dagger} is the canonical example. We emphasize that a least-squares right-inverse prescribes the behavior of A​BAB on all of ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}, but does not require BB to map into ker⁡(A)⟂\ker(A)^{\perp}.

Condition 2.22.

Let A:ℝN→ℝMA\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} be a linear operator and PIP_{I} be a projection operator on ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}. Let further XX be a square-integrable RV on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}. Assume the following hold:

  1. 1.

    BI:ℝM→ℝNB_{I}\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N} is a least-squares right-inverse of PI∘AP_{I}\circ A.

  2. 2.

    ϵI\epsilon_{I} denotes a RV on ℝI\mathbb{R}^{I} independent of A​XAX, with ϵ∥≔Pran(PI​A)​(ϵI)\epsilon_{\parallel}\coloneqq P_{\range(P_{I}A)}(\epsilon_{I}) and ϵ⟂≔Pran(PI​A)⟂​(ϵI)\epsilon_{\perp}\coloneqq P_{\range(P_{I}A)^{\perp}}(\epsilon_{I}) independent of each other.

Note that AA is not assumed to be injective; injectivity is needed only for the image-domain statement in Corollary 2.30. Condition 2.22.2 is satisfied for i.i.d. Gaussian noise, for which orthogonal projections onto complementary subspaces are independent. For non-Gaussian noise, uncorrelatedness of ϵ∥\epsilon_{\parallel} and ϵ⟂\epsilon_{\perp} does not imply their independence in general. In particular, the Poisson noise used in our experiments satisfies the condition only approximately: even in a high-dose regime, where it is well approximated by an additive Gaussian, the variance depends on the signal, so that ϵI\epsilon_{I} is not independent of A​XAX; see Section 3.

Theorem 2.23.

Assume Condition 2.22 holds, and denote by Fac(A,BI):={A∘f∘BI:f:ℝN→ℝN measurable}\Fac(A,B_{I}):=\bigl\{A\circ f\circ B_{I}\;:\;f\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}\text{ measurable}\bigr\} the class of all factorized reconstruction maps. Then minimizing the full self-supervised risk over Fac⁡(A,BI)\Fac(A,B_{I}) recovers the conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]=arg​ming∈Fac⁡(A,BI)⁡𝔼​[∥g⁡(YI)−AX∥22].\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=\argmin_{g\in\Fac(A,B_{I})}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].
Proof.

Write arg​ming∈Fac⁡(A,BI)⁡𝔼​[∥g⁡(YI)−AX∥22]=A∘f∗∘BI\argmin_{g\in\Fac(A,B_{I})}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=A\circ f^{*}\circ B_{I} with f∗=arg​minf⁡𝔼​[∥Af⁡(BI​(YI))−AX∥22]f^{*}=\argmin_{f}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert Af(B_{I}(Y_{I}))-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr], the right-hand sides being representatives of the respective arg​min\argmin sets. The objective depends on ff only through the composed map A∘fA\circ f. As ff ranges over all measurable maps ℝN→ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}, the quantity A​f​(BI​(YI))Af(B_{I}(Y_{I})) ranges over all σ⁡(BI​(YI))\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I}))-measurable, square-integrable RVs with values in ran(A)\range(A). Since ran(A)\range(A) is a linear subspace and A​XAX takes values in it, so does 𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]. Projection in L2L^{2} onto the σ⁡(BI​(YI))\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I}))-measurable random vectors therefore gives

arg​minu​σ​(BI​(YI))​-meas.,u∈ran(A)⁡𝔼​[‖u−AX‖22]=𝔼⁡[AX∣BI​(YI)],\argmin_{u\;\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I}))\text{-meas.},\;u\in\range(A)}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|u-AX\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})],

and this value is attained by f∗=A†𝔼[AX∣BI(YI)=⋅]f^{\ast}=A^{\dagger}\,\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})=\,\cdot\,], with A†A^{\dagger} the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, since A​A†=Pran(A)AA^{\dagger}=P_{\range(A)} acts as the identity on ran(A)\range(A). Hence any minimizer satisfies A∘f∗∘BI​(YI)=𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]almost surelyA\circ f^{*}\circ B_{I}(Y_{I})=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]\quad\text{almost surely}. No injectivity of AA is used; without it f∗f^{\ast} is determined only up to ker⁡(A)\ker(A), which is Corollary 2.30. It remains to show 𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]. Since A​XAX is independent of ϵI\epsilon_{I} and ϵ∥\epsilon_{\parallel} is independent of ϵ⟂\epsilon_{\perp}, the triple (A​X,ϵ∥,ϵ⟂)(AX,\epsilon_{\parallel},\epsilon_{\perp}) has a product law. Hence ϵ⟂\epsilon_{\perp} is independent of (A​X,ϵ∥)(AX,\epsilon_{\parallel}), therefore also of (A​X,PI​(A​X)+ϵ∥)(AX,P_{I}(AX)+\epsilon_{\parallel}), and

𝔼[AX∣YI]=𝔼[AX∣PI(AX)+ϵ∥,ϵ⟂]=𝔼[AX∣PI(AX)+ϵ∥]=𝔼[AX∣Pran(PI​A)(YI)].\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid P_{I}(AX)+\epsilon_{\parallel},\epsilon_{\perp}]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid P_{I}(AX)+\epsilon_{\parallel}]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid P_{\range(P_{I}A)}(Y_{I})].

The least-squares right-inverse property 2.22.1 implies σ⁡(Pran(PI​A)​(YI))⊆σ⁡(BI​(YI))⊆σ⁡(YI)\sigma(P_{\range(P_{I}A)}(Y_{I}))\subseteq\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I}))\subseteq\sigma(Y_{I}), since Pran(PI​A)​(YI)=(PI​A)​BI​(YI)P_{\range(P_{I}A)}(Y_{I})=(P_{I}A)\,B_{I}(Y_{I}) is a measurable function of BI​(YI)B_{I}(Y_{I}). This is where the least-squares property is needed: YIY_{I} lies outside ran(PI​A)\range(P_{I}A) because of ϵ⟂\epsilon_{\perp}, and the standard right-inverse property would not suffice (Remark 2.27). Thus 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] is σ⁡(BI​(YI))\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I}))-measurable, and the tower property yields 𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]|BI​(YI)]=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]\;\big|\;B_{I}(Y_{I})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}], which completes the proof. ∎

Remark 2.24 (Minimal condition on BIB_{I}).

The least-squares right-inverse property 2.22.1 enters the proof only through the inclusion σ⁡(Pran(PI​A)​(YI))⊆σ⁡(BI​(YI))\sigma(P_{\range(P_{I}A)}(Y_{I}))\subseteq\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I})), which together with 2.22.2 gives 𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]. The minimal condition for that identity is that BI​(YI)B_{I}(Y_{I}) be a sufficient statistic for A​XAX, i.e. that A​XAX and YIY_{I} be conditionally independent given BI​(YI)B_{I}(Y_{I}): BIB_{I} must not discard information about A​XAX contained in YIY_{I}.

The next proposition quantifies what an inexact initial reconstruction costs, complementing Theorem 2.17, which measures an inexact coverage condition.

Proposition 2.25 (The price of the factorized class).

Let AA be linear, let BI:ℝM→ℝNB_{I}\colon\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N} be measurable and let Z=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]Z=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]. Then

ming∈Fac⁡(A,BI)⁡𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22]−ming​σ​(YI)​-meas.⁡𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥Z−𝔼⁡[Z|BI​(YI)]∥22].\min_{g\in\Fac(A,B_{I})}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]\;-\;\min_{g\;\sigma(Y_{I})\text{-meas.}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert Z-\mathbb{E}\bigl[Z\bigm|B_{I}(Y_{I})\bigr]\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].

The restriction to Fac⁡(A,BI)\Fac(A,B_{I}) thus costs exactly the part of ZZ that BI​(YI)B_{I}(Y_{I}) does not determine, and nothing when BI​(YI)B_{I}(Y_{I}) is sufficient for A​XAX.

Proof.

By the argument in the proof of Theorem 2.23, which uses no property of BIB_{I}, every minimizer over Fac⁡(A,BI)\Fac(A,B_{I}) satisfies A​f∗​(BI​(YI))=𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]Af^{\ast}(B_{I}(Y_{I}))=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})] almost surely, and since σ⁡(BI​(YI))⊆σ⁡(YI)\sigma(B_{I}(Y_{I}))\subseteq\sigma(Y_{I}) the tower property gives 𝔼⁡[A​X∣BI​(YI)]=𝔼⁡[Z∣BI​(YI)]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})]. The Pythagoras identity for conditional expectations applied twice yields 𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−A​X∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−Z∥22]+σ2\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-Z\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]+\sigma^{2} with σ2=𝔼⁡[∥A​X−Z∥22]\sigma^{2}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert AX-Z\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr] for every σ⁡(YI)\sigma(Y_{I})-measurable gg. Taking g=𝔼⁡[Z∣BI​(YI)]g=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid B_{I}(Y_{I})] and g=Zg=Z and subtracting gives the claim. ∎

Remark 2.26 (What the criterion targets).

All results of this section identify the conditional expectation, that is, the minimum mean squared error estimator. This is the estimator that maximizes PSNR, and it is the natural target for a criterion built on a squared loss, but it is a choice rather than a necessity: the conditional expectation averages over all images consistent with YIY_{I} and is therefore systematically smoothing. Where low-contrast detectability rather than mean squared error is the quantity of interest, a different criterion, and correspondingly a different notion of optimality, would be appropriate. The equivalence between the partially self-supervised and the full self-supervised risk established here is independent of that choice in the following sense: it compares two ways of estimating the same objective, and any weighted quadratic objective would give the same argument. The equivalence established here is independent of that choice: it compares two ways of estimating the same objective, and any weighted quadratic objective gives the same argument.

Remark 2.27 (Necessity of the least-squares property).

If BB does not control (PI​A)​B(P_{I}A)B outside ran(PI​A)\range(P_{I}A), then B⁡(YI)B(Y_{I}) can contain less information about PI​(A​X)P_{I}(AX) than YIY_{I}, and Theorem 2.23 fails. Let

A=(10),PI=I2,B⁡(x1,x2)=x1+x2.A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_{I}=I_{2},\qquad B(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}+x_{2}.

Then PI​A​X=A​X=(X,0)⊤P_{I}AX=AX=(X,0)^{\top}, and BB is a right-inverse of PI​AP_{I}A in the standard sense, since (PI​A)​B​y=y(P_{I}A)By=y for all y=(y1,0)⊤∈ran(PI​A)y=(y_{1},0)^{\top}\in\range(P_{I}A). However, BB is not a least-squares right-inverse: for y=(0,y2)⊤∉ran(PI​A)y=(0,y_{2})^{\top}\not\in\range(P_{I}A) we have (PI​A)​B​y=(y2,0)⊤≠0=Pran(PI​A)​(y)(P_{I}A)By=(y_{2},0)^{\top}\neq 0=P_{\range(P_{I}A)}(y).
Consider the observation model YI=A​X+ϵ=(X+ϵ1,ϵ2)⊤Y_{I}=AX+\epsilon=(X+\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2})^{\top}, where X,ϵ1,ϵ2X,\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2} are independent standard Gaussian random variables. Then YIY_{I} contains the two independent noisy observations X+ϵ1X+\epsilon_{1} and ϵ2\epsilon_{2}, whereas B⁡(YI)=X+ϵ1+ϵ2B(Y_{I})=X+\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2} only contains their sum. Consequently, 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]≠𝔼⁡[A​X∣B⁡(YI)]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]\neq\mathbb{E}[AX\mid B(Y_{I})].

For the Radon transform the FBP is not a right-inverse of PI∘AP_{I}\circ A, not even in the standard sense: restricting AA by PIP_{I}, or merely discretizing it, removes information, so that PI​A​B​(y)≠yP_{I}AB(y)\neq y in general even for y∈ran(PI​A)y\in\range(P_{I}A).

Combining Theorem 2.23 with the equivariant construction of Section 2.3 closes the gap between the generic equivariant class of Theorem 2.11 and the architecture used in practice.

Corollary 2.28 (Equivariant architectures suffice).

Assume Conditions 2.9, 2.18 (with B=BIB=B_{I}), and 2.22 hold, and denote by

Equi(A,BI;𝒮):={A∘f∘BI:f:ℝN→ℝN measurable and 𝒮-equivariant}\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S}):=\bigl\{A\circ f\circ B_{I}\;:\;f\colon\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}\text{ measurable and }\mathcal{S}\text{-equivariant}\bigr\}

the equivariant subclass. Then minimizing the full self-supervised risk over Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S}) recovers the conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]=arg​ming∈Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)⁡𝔼​[∥g⁡(YI)−AX∥22].\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=\argmin_{g\in\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S})}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-AX\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].
Proof.

Let f∗f^{*} be the minimizer from the proof of Theorem 2.23, so that g∗≔A∘f∗∘BIg^{*}\coloneqq A\circ f^{*}\circ B_{I} satisfies g∗​(YI)=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]g^{*}(Y_{I})=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] almost surely, and define the symmetrization f~≔1L​∑ℓ=1LSℓ−1∘f∗∘Sℓ\tilde{f}\coloneqq\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}S_{\ell}^{-1}\circ f^{*}\circ S_{\ell}, which is 𝒮\mathcal{S}-equivariant by Theorem 2.20 (applied with Φ=f∗\Phi=f^{*}). The intertwining relations of Condition 2.18 give A​Sℓ−1=Tℓ−1​AAS_{\ell}^{-1}=T_{\ell}^{-1}A and Sℓ​BI=BI​TℓS_{\ell}B_{I}=B_{I}T_{\ell}, hence

A∘f~∘BI=1L​∑ℓ=1L(A​Sℓ−1)∘f∗∘(Sℓ​BI)=1L​∑ℓ=1LTℓ−1∘(A∘f∗∘BI)∘Tℓ=1L​∑ℓ=1LTℓ−1∘g∗∘Tℓ.A\circ\tilde{f}\circ B_{I}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(AS_{\ell}^{-1})\circ f^{*}\circ(S_{\ell}B_{I})=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}T_{\ell}^{-1}\circ(A\circ f^{*}\circ B_{I})\circ T_{\ell}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}T_{\ell}^{-1}\circ g^{*}\circ T_{\ell}.

By (A6) and Lemma 2.7 (with Y=A​XY=AX), g∗g^{*} is TℓT_{\ell}-equivariant πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-a.e., so Tℓ−1∘g∗∘Tℓ=g∗T_{\ell}^{-1}\circ g^{*}\circ T_{\ell}=g^{*} πYI\pi_{Y_{I}}-a.e. for every ℓ\ell and hence A∘f~∘BI​(YI)=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]A\circ\tilde{f}\circ B_{I}(Y_{I})=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] almost surely. The minimal value of Theorem 2.23 is therefore attained within Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)⊆Fac⁡(A,BI)\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S})\subseteq\Fac(A,B_{I}). A pointwise equivariant representative is provided by Lemma 2.8. ∎

Corollary 2.29 (Main result).

Assume Conditions 2.9, 2.18 (with B=BIB=B_{I}) and 2.22 hold. Then

𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]=arg​ming∈Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)⁡𝔼​[∥PS​g​(YI)−YS∥22].\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=\argmin_{g\in\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S})}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}\,g(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr].
Proof.

By Theorem 2.20, every g=A∘f∘BIg=A\circ f\circ B_{I} with 𝒮\mathcal{S}-equivariant ff is 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant, hence Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)⊆Equi⁡(ℝM;𝒯)\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S})\subseteq\Equi(\mathbb{R}^{M};\mathcal{T}). By Corollary 2.13 applied to 𝒞=Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)\mathcal{C}=\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S}), minimizing the partially self-supervised noisy risk over this class is equivalent to minimizing 𝔼⁡[∥g⁡(YI)−𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]∥22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert g(Y_{I})-\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr] over the same class. By Corollary 2.28 the value 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] is attained within Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S}), so this minimum equals zero and is attained precisely at 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]. ∎

Corollary 2.29 closes the chain from the training objective to the optimal predictor: no ground-truth image, no fully sampled measurement and no noise-free target enters, and yet the minimizer over the trained architecture class is the conditional expectation given the undersampled data. The following corollary transfers the statement from the measurement domain, in which the loss is formulated, to the image domain, in which reconstructions are evaluated.

Corollary 2.30 (Image-domain optimality up to the null space).

Under the assumptions of Corollary 2.29, let g∗=A∘f∗∘BIg^{\ast}=A\circ f^{\ast}\circ B_{I} be a minimizer of the partially self-supervised risk over Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S}). Then the learned reconstruction map satisfies

Pker⁡(A)⟂​f∗​(BI​(YI))=Pker⁡(A)⟂​𝔼​[X∣YI]almost surely.P_{\ker(A)^{\perp}}f^{\ast}\bigl(B_{I}(Y_{I})\bigr)=P_{\ker(A)^{\perp}}\,\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y_{I}]\qquad\text{almost surely}.

If in addition AA is injective, then f∗​(BI​(YI))=𝔼⁡[X∣YI]f^{\ast}(B_{I}(Y_{I}))=\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y_{I}] almost surely, i.e. ELIPPS training returns the minimum mean squared error estimator of the image given the undersampled measurements.

Proof.

By Corollary 2.29 and linearity of AA, A​f∗​(BI​(YI))=𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]=A​𝔼​[X∣YI]Af^{\ast}(B_{I}(Y_{I}))=\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}]=A\,\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y_{I}] almost surely, so the difference f∗​(BI​(YI))−𝔼⁡[X∣YI]f^{\ast}(B_{I}(Y_{I}))-\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y_{I}] lies in ker⁡(A)\ker(A); applying Pker⁡(A)⟂P_{\ker(A)^{\perp}} gives the first claim, and injectivity means ker⁡(A)={0}\ker(A)=\{0\}. ∎

Remark 2.31 (The null space is not identified by the risk alone).

Corollary 2.30 is sharp: the training risk depends on A​f∘BIAf\circ B_{I} only, so no criterion of this form determines the component in ker⁡(A)\ker(A). For the discretized Radon transform of Section 3, which maps 3612=130 321361^{2}=130\,321 pixels to 128×361=46 208128\times 361=46\,208 measurements, the image-domain statement therefore holds only modulo ker⁡(A)\ker(A). What constrains that component in practice is the hypothesis class: the equivariance of fθf_{\theta}, the choice of BIB_{I} and the implicit bias of the network. Combining the sensing theorems of [18, 13] with the present setting is a natural next step.

Remark 2.32 (Biased supervision within the factorized class).

For the constrained class Equi⁡(A,BI,𝒮)\Equi(A,B_{I};\mathcal{S}), Remark 2.12 needs one qualification: its elements take values in ran(A)\range(A), whereas 𝔼⁡[A​X+β⁡(X)∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX+\beta(X)\mid Y_{I}] need not, so the attainability step of Corollary 2.29 may fail. Consistency is unaffected, since by Corollary 2.13 training returns the L2L^{2}-projection of the shifted target onto the realized class. The qualification is vacuous when ran(A)=ℝM\range(A)=\mathbb{R}^{M}, the expected situation in Section 3.

Remark 2.33 (Role of Condition 2.22).

The two conditions play different roles. Condition 2.9 concerns the training criterion: by Corollary 2.13 it makes the partially self-supervised risk rank equivariant candidates exactly as the full self-supervised risk does, for every hypothesis class. Condition 2.22 concerns the hypothesis class: it keeps the optimum from being excluded by the factorized architecture. If it is violated, training still returns the best approximation of 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}] within the realized class, so misspecification causes an approximation error, never an inconsistent target. The experiments in Section 3 operate in that regime.

Remark 2.34 (The two requirements on BIB_{I} are compatible).

Condition 2.18.2 and Condition 2.22.1 constrain the same operator, and it is not immediate that they can be met at once. They can, and the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the subsampled forward operator is the canonical example. Assume the TℓT_{\ell} and SℓS_{\ell} are orthogonal, Tℓ​A=A​SℓT_{\ell}A=AS_{\ell}, and PI​Tℓ=Tℓ​PIP_{I}T_{\ell}=T_{\ell}P_{I}, and put M:=PI​AM:=P_{I}A. Then

M​Sℓ=PI​A​Sℓ=PI​Tℓ​A=Tℓ​PI​A=Tℓ​M,MS_{\ell}=P_{I}AS_{\ell}=P_{I}T_{\ell}A=T_{\ell}P_{I}A=T_{\ell}M,

so M=Tℓ​M​Sℓ−1M=T_{\ell}MS_{\ell}^{-1}. Since (U​M​V)†=V∗​M†​U∗(UMV)^{\dagger}=V^{\ast}M^{\dagger}U^{\ast} for unitary U,VU,V, this gives M†=Sℓ​M†​Tℓ−1M^{\dagger}=S_{\ell}M^{\dagger}T_{\ell}^{-1}, that is M†​Tℓ=Sℓ​M†M^{\dagger}T_{\ell}=S_{\ell}M^{\dagger}. Hence BI:=(PI​A)†B_{I}:=(P_{I}A)^{\dagger} intertwines as required by Condition 2.18.2 The same argument covers truncated Krylov methods on the normal equations, since M⊤​M​Sℓ=Sℓ​M⊤​MM^{\!\top}MS_{\ell}=S_{\ell}M^{\!\top}M. In Section 3 the TℓT_{\ell} are signed coordinate permutations and the SℓS_{\ell} coordinate permutations, so the assumptions of Corollary 2.29 are jointly satisfiable; the FBP used there gives up 1 for computational convenience, which by Remark 2.33 costs accuracy and not consistency.

2.5 Summary of the method

Suppose the image model satisfies Conditions 2.9 and 2.22 with transforms satisfying Condition 2.18, and let (Φθ)θ∈Θ(\Phi_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta} be any image-space network. According to Theorem 2.20 the functions fθ=1L​∑ℓSℓ−1∘Φθ∘Sℓf_{\theta}=\tfrac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell}S_{\ell}^{-1}\circ\Phi_{\theta}\circ S_{\ell} and gθ=A∘fθ∘Bg_{\theta}=A\circ f_{\theta}\circ B are 𝒮\mathcal{S}- and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-equivariant, respectively. By Theorem 2.23 and Corollary 2.28 this restriction costs nothing when BB is a least-squares right-inverse of PI∘AP_{I}\circ A, and Corollary 2.29 gives the statement used in practice: the minimizer of the partially self-supervised noisy risk over this class is 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}], and by Corollary 2.30 the reconstruction fθ∘Bf_{\theta}\circ B agrees with the minimum mean squared error estimator up to ker⁡(A)\ker(A). For an approximate inverse such as the FBP, Remark 2.33 shows that only the expressivity of the class is affected, not the correctness of the criterion. The training itself uses only the partial self-supervision data (1.2), through

ℒ𝒯​(θ)=𝔼⁡[∥PS∘gθ​(YI)−YS∥22]=𝔼⁡[∥AS∘fθ∘B⁡(YI)−YS∥22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{T}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert P_{S}\circ g_{\theta}(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert A_{S}\circ f_{\theta}\circ B(Y_{I})-Y_{S}\rVert_{2}^{2}\bigr]. (2.5)

At test time, the reconstruction is simply obtained by the learned reconstruction maps fθ∘Bf_{\theta}\circ B.

3 Experiments

This section evaluates ELIPPS under severe partial self-supervision and low-dose noise. We consider two instantiations of the undersampled inverse problem (1.1) in CT, which differ only in the axis along which the sinogram is subsampled:

  • •

    Detector Upscaling: only a subset of detector bins is observed; the goal is to recover the full-resolution measurement and a corresponding reconstruction.

  • •

    Sparse-View Reconstruction: only a subset of projection angles is observed; the goal is to recover a high-quality reconstruction from angularly undersampled measurements.

In both settings, we instantiate the transformation families 𝒯\mathcal{T} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} of Section 2.2 via the eight symmetries of the dihedral group

D4={Id,r,r2,r3,σ,r​σ,r2​σ,r3​σ},D_{4}=\{\operatorname{Id},\,r,\,r^{2},\,r^{3},\,\sigma,\,r\sigma,\,r^{2}\sigma,\,r^{3}\sigma\}, (3.1)

where rr is the rotation by 90∘90^{\circ} and σ\sigma the reflection about the vertical image axis. The group D4D_{4} acts on the image domain by rotations and reflections of the pixel grid and, via the intertwining relation with the Radon transform, on the measurement domain by permutations of the sinogram coordinates. This makes the abstract framework of Section 2.2 fully explicit: we verify Conditions 2.9 and 2.18 for this instantiation below.

3.1 Dataset and Acquisition Model

We use a 1%1\% subset of the LoDoPaB dataset [23], consisting of 358358 training and 3535 test images. Unless stated otherwise (see the ablation in Section 3.7), the training set is augmented by the full D4D_{4} group, yielding an 8×8\times larger training set whose empirical distribution is D4D_{4}-invariant by construction. All images are resized to 361×361361\times 361 pixels and multiplied by a circular disk mask restricting the reconstruction to the field of view. Here 361361 is the side length of the grid, so the image has 3612=130 321361^{2}=130\,321 pixels. Both the side length and the number of detector bins are odd, so that a single central pixel and a single central detector bin exist and are fixed by the discrete D4D_{4} action; this is what makes the rotations and reflections exact permutations of the grids. The circular field of view is the disc inscribed in that grid and is therefore 361361 pixels across. The disk mask is D4D_{4}-invariant and therefore compatible with the invariance assumptions of Condition 2.9.

We adopt a parallel-beam geometry with Nθ=128N_{\theta}=128 projection angles on the endpoint-exclusive grid θj=j​π/Nθ\theta_{j}=j\pi/N_{\theta}, j=0,…,Nθ−1j=0,\dots,N_{\theta}-1, and Ns=361N_{s}=361 detector bins, yielding dense sinograms of size 128×361128\times 361. The angular spacing π/Nθ\pi/N_{\theta} is chosen such that π/2\pi/2 is an integer multiple of it, which is what makes the rotations of D4D_{4} exact permutations of the sinogram grid; this fails, for instance, for Nθ=129N_{\theta}=129. To simulate low-dose acquisition we use the count model of the LoDoPaB benchmark. With base photon count λ=1000\lambda=1000 and attenuation factor μ=2.76\mu=2.76, the dimensionless product of the linear attenuation coefficient of the LoDoPaB forward model with the field of view under our normalization of A​xAx, the detected counts along each ray are

N∼𝒫⁡(λ​e−μ​A​x),yδ=−1μ​log⁡(max⁡{N,1}/λ),N\sim\mathcal{P}\bigl(\lambda\,e^{-\mu Ax}\bigr),\qquad y^{\delta}=-\tfrac{1}{\mu}\,\log\bigl(\max\{N,1\}/\lambda\bigr), (3.2)

where the clipping of the counts from below keeps the logarithm well defined. All Poisson-corrupted sinograms below are generated by (3.2).

3.2 D4D_{4}-Equivariance and Explicit Operator Relations

We now instantiate 𝒯=(Tℓ)ℓ=18\mathcal{T}=(T_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{8} in the measurement domain and the corresponding image-domain transforms 𝒮=(Sℓ)ℓ=18\mathcal{S}=(S_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{8}, and verify the intertwining relations of Condition 2.18.

Radon transform and orthogonal transforms:

Let the parallel-beam Radon transform be discretized as A∈ℝ(Nθ​Ns)×(Nx​Ny)A\in\mathbb{R}^{(N_{\theta}N_{s})\times(N_{x}N_{y})}, so that A​x∈ℝNθ×NsAx\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\theta}\times N_{s}} is the sinogram of x∈ℝNx×Nyx\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{x}\times N_{y}}. Let Q∈O⁡(2)Q\in O(2) map the image grid onto itself, so that i↦Q−1​ii\mapsto Q^{-1}i is a permutation of the pixel indices, and write SQS_{Q} for the corresponding permutation matrix, (SQ​x)i=xQ−1​i(S_{Q}x)_{i}=x_{Q^{-1}i}. Assume further that QQ maps the sinogram grid onto itself, through nθ′=Q⊤​nθn_{\theta^{\prime}}=Q^{\top}n_{\theta} with nθ=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)⊤n_{\theta}=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^{\top} and, whenever θ′∉[0,π)\theta^{\prime}\notin[0,\pi), the Radon symmetry (A​x)θ+π,s=(A​x)θ,−s(Ax)_{\theta+\pi,\,s}=(Ax)_{\theta,\,-s}; write TQT_{Q} for the resulting permutation matrix. A change of variables in the continuous Radon transform then gives

A​SQ=TQ​A.AS_{Q}=T_{Q}A. (3.3)

Both assumptions hold for the elements of D4D_{4} with the grid sizes fixed above, since Ns=361N_{s}=361 is odd and π/2\pi/2 is an integer multiple of π/Nθ\pi/N_{\theta} with Nθ=128N_{\theta}=128.

D4D_{4} instantiation:

Let D4⊆O⁡(2)D_{4}\subseteq O(2) consist of the four rotations Rk​π/2R_{k\pi/2} and the four reflections Rk​π/2​FR_{k\pi/2}F, k∈{0,1,2,3}k\in\{0,1,2,3\}, where

Rα=(cos⁡α−sin⁡αsin⁡αcos⁡α),F=(−1001).R_{\alpha}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\ \sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}.

Each element maps both grids onto itself, so that (3.3) applies. Indexing them as Q1,…,Q8Q_{1},\dots,Q_{8} and writing Sℓ:=SQℓS_{\ell}:=S_{Q_{\ell}} and Tℓ:=TQℓT_{\ell}:=T_{Q_{\ell}} gives the families 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} of Condition 2.18. A rotation by k​π/2k\pi/2 shifts the angular axis, a reflection reverses it: (Tk​y)θ,s=yθ−k​π/2,s(T_{k}\,y)_{\theta,s}=y_{\theta-k\pi/2,\;s} and (Tk+4​y)θ,s=yπ−θ+k​π/2,s(T_{k+4}\,y)_{\theta,s}=y_{\pi-\theta+k\pi/2,\;s}. Any index that leaves [0,π)[0,\pi) is brought back by yθ+π,s=yθ,−sy_{\theta+\pi,\,s}=y_{\theta,\,-s}, which flips the detector axis. All indices are modulo the grid size.

Verification of Condition 2.18:

The relations above yield the intertwining Tℓ​A=A​SℓT_{\ell}A=AS_{\ell} for ℓ=1,…,8\ell=1,\dots,8, i.e., Condition 2.18.1. Since (Sℓ)ℓ=18(S_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{8} is the permutation representation of D4D_{4} and hence a group of order eight, Condition 2.18.3 holds as well. Finally, the filtered backprojection intertwines with rotations and reflections of the image grid, since both the backprojection and the (radially symmetric) filtering step commute with the induced sinogram permutations; this gives B​Tℓ=Sℓ​BBT_{\ell}=S_{\ell}B and thus Condition 2.18.2.

3.3 Observation and Masking

Acquisition model:

For each training sample, we generate two conditionally independent noisy full sinograms according to (3.2), written 𝒫1​(A​x)\mathcal{P}_{1}(Ax) and 𝒫2​(A​x)\mathcal{P}_{2}(Ax) for brevity, and apply the input and supervision sampling operators separately:

yIδ=PI(𝒫1(Ax)),ySδ=PS(𝒫2(Ax)),𝒫1⟂𝒫2∣x.y_{I}^{\delta}=P_{I}\left(\mathcal{P}_{1}(Ax)\right),\qquad y_{S}^{\delta}=P_{S}\left(\mathcal{P}_{2}(Ax)\right),\qquad\mathcal{P}_{1}\perp\mathcal{P}_{2}\mid x. (3.4)

Here II denotes the task-dependent input sampling set, while SS is the fixed supervision set defined below. Because the input and supervision measurements are generated from independent Poisson realizations, their conditional independence is preserved even when I∩S≠∅I\cap S\neq\varnothing. As shown in Remark 2.10, this conditional independence is the structure required by (A4), and it is compatible with signal-dependent noise; the remaining discrepancy in our simulation is the bias of the log transform, quantified below. Only PIP_{I} of the first realization and PSP_{S} of the second are ever used, so the training acquisition is cheaper than two full scans. The relevant count is projections rather than measurements, since a projection irradiates the whole slice: for detector upscaling the input uses all 128128 angles and the supervision a further 3232, i.e. 1.251.25 times the deployment scan, whereas for sparse-view reconstruction the input and supervision angles overlap in only 88 of 3232, so that 6464 projections are needed and the factor is exactly two. A disjoint design I∩S=∅I\cap S=\emptyset would give the conditional centring of (A4) from a single scan, because Poisson noise is independent across detector coordinates, but it is incompatible with the remaining assumptions: if PI​Tℓ=Tℓ​PIP_{I}T_{\ell}=T_{\ell}P_{I} for every ℓ\ell, then II is a union of 𝒯\mathcal{T}-orbits, while (A7) applied to v=epv=e_{p} for p∈Ip\in I gives ∑ℓ‖PS​Tℓ​ep‖22=c>0\sum_{\ell}\|P_{S}T_{\ell}e_{p}\|_{2}^{2}=c>0 and hence Tℓ​p∈ST_{\ell}\,p\in S for some ℓ\ell; since Tℓ​pT_{\ell}\,p lies in the orbit of pp, it lies in II, so that I∩S≠∅I\cap S\neq\emptyset. The two structural assumptions of Condition 2.9 therefore force the input and supervision sets to overlap.

What does realize partial self-supervision from a single scan, at unchanged total photon budget and also on an overlap, is Poisson thinning: splitting the detected count NN as N=N1+N2N=N_{1}+N_{2} with N1|N∼Bin⁡(N,1/2)N_{1}\mid N\sim\mathrm{Bin}(N,1/2) yields two exactly independent Poisson variables of half the rate, from which yIδy_{I}^{\delta} and ySδy_{S}^{\delta} are formed by (3.2) with λ\lambda replaced by λ/2\lambda/2. The reported experiments use (3.4), which has the same structure at the increased dose quantified above. Thinning halves the counts in both measurements and therefore changes the operating point of every method compared, so all baselines would have to be retrained; we describe it as the dose-neutral realization of the setting rather than reporting it here.

Poisson noise and the log transform:

Under the count model (3.2) the supervision measurement is not unbiased: a second-order expansion of the logarithm around the mean count gives

𝔼⁡[yδ|x]=A​x+β⁡(x),β⁡(x)≈12​μ​λeff​(x),λeff​(x)=λ​e−μ​A​x,\mathbb{E}\bigl[y^{\delta}\bigm|x\bigr]=Ax+\beta(x),\qquad\beta(x)\approx\frac{1}{2\mu\,\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}(x)},\qquad\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}(x)=\lambda\,e^{-\mu Ax},

so that (A4) holds only up to β\beta. The clipping of zero counts is inactive at this dose: the smallest effective count is λ​e−μ≈63\lambda e^{-\mu}\approx 63, so that ℙ⁡(N=0)\mathbb{P}(N=0) is of order 10−2810^{-28} and no zero count occurs anywhere in the data; it is retained for numerical safety and starts to contribute below λ≈200\lambda\approx 200. The bias is largest where the expected count is smallest. On the data set used here the sinograms are normalized by their maximum, so that A​x∈[0,1]Ax\in[0,1] with mean 0.360.36 on the training and 0.440.44 on the test split; the corresponding effective counts are λeff≈370\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 370 and ≈290\approx 290, giving β≈4.9⋅10−4\beta\approx 4.9\cdot 10^{-4} and β≈6.2⋅10−4\beta\approx 6.2\cdot 10^{-4}. For the most strongly attenuated rays, with λeff=λ​e−μ≈63\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}=\lambda e^{-\mu}\approx 63, it reaches β≈2.9⋅10−3\beta\approx 2.9\cdot 10^{-3}; the normalization makes this worst case attained. Even the worst case is more than two orders of magnitude below the attenuation values it perturbs. By Remark 2.12 this does not invalidate the training criterion: Theorem 2.11 then identifies 𝔼⁡[A​X+β⁡(X)∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX+\beta(X)\mid Y_{I}] rather than 𝔼⁡[A​X∣YI]\mathbb{E}[AX\mid Y_{I}], so the bias of the supervision measurement is inherited by the learned predictor.
